text: You have built retrieval-augmented systems already: embed the question, find similar chunks, and paste them into the prompt. This lesson looks underneath that recipe, at why it works, where it quietly fails, and what the model is actually doing with the text you hand it.

A language model stores knowledge in its weights, which is called parametric memory, and that memory is fixed at training time, hazy about rare facts and impossible to cite. The original retrieval-augmented generation paper, by Lewis and colleagues at Facebook in twenty twenty, paired a generator with a non-parametric memory, a searchable index of Wikipedia passages, so that knowledge can be changed by editing documents rather than by retraining. It is the difference between remembering a book and keeping it on the desk beside you.

Retrieval begins with an encoder that maps the question and every chunk into vectors in the same space, trained so that a question lands near the passages that answer it. Because each chunk is encoded on its own, without the question, its vector can be computed once and stored, and finding the best matches becomes a nearest-neighbour search by cosine similarity, which is just a dot product once every vector has been scaled to unit length.

With millions of chunks, comparing the question against every one of them is too slow, so vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes. A popular one, called HNSW, links each vector to its neighbours in layered graphs and searches them greedily, rather like finding a house by taking the motorway first, then the main roads, then the side streets. It accepts a small chance of missing the true best match in exchange for a very large gain in speed.

Squeezing a whole question into one vector throws detail away, so careful systems add a second stage. A cross-encoder reads the question and a candidate chunk together and scores how well they fit, which is more accurate and far too slow to run on everything, so it only reranks the top few dozen candidates. Many systems also blend dense search with keyword search such as BM25, because exact names and codes are often where embeddings are weakest.

Once the chunks are in the prompt, nothing special happens to them: they are simply tokens in the context, and attention lets each generated token draw on them, just as it draws on any earlier text. That is why retrieval quality matters so much. The model cannot use a fact that was never retrieved, and it reads a plausible but wrong chunk as readily as a right one. Position matters too. In a study titled Lost in the Middle, Liu and colleagues found that models often used information best when it sat near the beginning or the end of a long context, and noticeably worse when it sat in the middle.

So a retrieval system deserves to be measured in two parts. First, recall at k: across questions whose answers you know, how often does a passage containing the answer appear among the top k results? Then, given good passages, is the answer faithful to them? Keeping the two apart tells you whether to fix the search or the generation.

Retrieval gives a model knowledge it was never trained on, but only as text to read. The next lesson goes one step further and lets the model act, by calling tools and reading their results, which is the mechanism behind agents.
